newsitem.title: DUBAI: Haj blaze kills 217, injures 1,290 in Saudi Arabia. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Haj blaze kills 217, injures 1,290 in Saudi Arabia. [CORRECTED 00:35 GMT]

text.p: Fire, starting from a cooking gas cylinder and fanned by high winds as it raced through a vast sea of tents, killed more than 200 Moslem pilgrims near the holy city of Mecca.

Most of the victims were reported to be from India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. They were among some two million Moslems from 100 countries gathering for the annual haj pilgrimage, which reaches its climax on Wednesday (corrects from "starts at dawn on Wednesday").

Saudi Arabia's state television reported the official toll early on Wednesday morning, saying that 217 people died and 1,290 were injured in the fire which broke out on Tuesday morning on the plain of Mena, about 11 km (seven miles) from Mecca.
The TV showed fire engines and ambulances with wailing sirens speeding to the scene as panic-stricken pilgrims fled the fire.
A frail old man was seen carried away on a stretcher. Helicopters sprayed the flames as clouds of black smoke filled the clear desert skies.

The plain, covered a few hours earlier by row after row of white tents, was turned into a charred wasteland under a haze of smoke. A swath more than two km (1.2 miles) long was flattened and littered with scorched debris. Saudi television said 70,000 tents were destroyed.
Diplomats and witnesses said the blaze had been caused by gas cylinder explosions. The TV showed security forces dragging gas cylinders away from the site of the blaze.
Lieutenant-General Mohammad bin Ali al-Suhaili, head of the Saudi civil defence forces, told the television many of the injured were in serious condition.
Pakistan's Ambassador Shahed Amin, who toured the site, told Reuters he saw tens of thousands of tents gutted by the flames.
Prince Majed, the governor of Mecca, ordered the speedy rebuilding of the camp, the official Saudi Press Agency said.
The fire, which broke out at 11.45 a.m. on Tuesday and spread quickly in high winds, had been extinguished by 3.05 p.m., Saudi media said.

The television said King Fahd had expressed condolences on his own and his country's behalf to the families of the victims from Saudi Arabia and abroad. There was no official breakdown of the victims' nationalities.
Indian deputy chief of mission in Riyadh, George Joseph, said many families were separated on their way to Mena, making it difficult to determine casualties.
"Now the dark of night makes the job even more difficult," one diplomat said.

Indian Ambassador Mohammad Hamad Ansari said: "A good many tents were burnt, including the Indian embassy control centre, which was completely gutted. A lot of people are left without shelter among the Indian pilgrims."
The fatal blaze is the latest tragedy to strike Moslems on pilgrimage to Mecca, their holiest shrine. Able-bodied Moslems are obliged to make the haj at least once if they can afford it.
The worst of recent Mecca tragedies was a stampede in 1990 in which 1,426 pilgrims were crushed to death in a tunnel. In 1994, 270 pilgrims were also killed during a stampede.
Saudi Arabia said three people were killed in 1995 when a fire swept through the tent camps in Mena. The fire had started when Saudis lit a stove in their tent and spread in strong wind.
Saudi Arabia, custodian of Islam's two holiest shrines, has spent $18.6 billion in the last decade on expanding pilgrimage sites in Mecca and surrounding areas.
Saudi officials had said they were doing their best to ensure a safe haj. They have urged the pilgrims to abide by security instructions, especially in congested areas.
Cameras installed on main roads, bridges and tunnels monitor pilgrims' movements to ensure that haj proceeds peacefully.
At dawn on Wednesday, pilgrims are due to march to Mount Arafat, where Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago, marking the climax of the haj.
